shots.src: US GAO, IMTEC-92-26 (1992): Patriot Missile Defense, Software Problem Led to System Failure at Dhahran
shots.narration: February twenty-fifth, 1991. Dhahran, Saudi Arabia. {p} An American Patriot missile battery is guarding a base. Its radar picks up an incoming Iraqi Scud missile. {pp} And then it does... nothing.

shots.src: US GAO, IMTEC-92-26 (1992): Patriot Missile Defense, Software Problem Led to System Failure at Dhahran
shots.title: February 25, 1991
shots.narration: The Scud hit an army barracks. Twenty-eight American soldiers were killed. {pp} The cause wasn't a broken part, and it wasn't a human mistake. {p} It was a number. {pp} One tenth.

This is a story about four tiny math errors. {p} A missile that missed. A rocket that blew itself up. A stock market that lost half its value for no reason. {p} And a bug that's still ticking inside billions of devices. {p} It all starts with something your computer gets wrong right now: zero point one, plus zero point two.

items.text: A rocket that blew itself up
A market that “lost” half its value

shots.title: any programming console
shots.src: IEEE 754 double precision (JavaScript, Python, Java, C...)
shots.narration: Open any programming console and type: zero point one, plus zero point two. {p} You'd expect zero point three. {pp} You get this. {p} Zero point three, then fifteen zeros, then a four.

shots.title: the same problem, in decimal
shots.narration: Your computer isn't broken. This is how almost every computer stores numbers: a standard called IEEE seven fifty-four. {p} And you already know the problem from school. {p} Try writing one third as a decimal. Zero point three three three three three... It never ends. {p} At some point you have to stop, and the moment you stop, you're slightly wrong.

lines.note: the 3s never end, so you have to stop somewhere

shots.label: 0.1 in binary

chop.text: no room left: the rest is thrown away

shots.narration: Computers count in binary, in ones and zeros. {p} And in binary, one tenth is just like one third: it never ends. {p} Zero point zero zero zero one one zero zero one one zero zero one one, forever. {p} So the computer keeps what fits, and chops off the rest.

shots.title: how wrong is it?
shots.narration: That chopped-off piece is the four at the end. {p} The error is tiny, about five hundred-quadrillionths. {p} Most of the time, nobody cares. {pp} Unless you add it up, millions of times. {p} Which is exactly what happened in Dhahran.

shots.title: add one tenth, ten times
shots.narration: Here's another way to see it. {p} Add one tenth to itself ten times. {p} You should get exactly one. {pp} You don't. {p} That's why banking software counts money in whole cents, as integers, where there's nothing to chop.

shots.src: US GAO, IMTEC-92-26 (1992): Patriot Missile Defense, Software Problem Led to System Failure at Dhahran · bits after the binary point
shots.label: 0.1 inside the Patriot
shots.narration: The Patriot's computer kept time by counting tenths of a second. {p} To turn that count into seconds, it multiplied by one tenth, stored in a register only twenty-four bits long. {p} So one tenth got chopped. {p} Every tick, the clock lost about ninety-five billionths of a second.

shots.src: US GAO, IMTEC-92-26 (1992): Patriot Missile Defense, Software Problem Led to System Failure at Dhahran
shots.narration: To see why that mattered, you need to know how a Patriot tracks a target. {p} The radar spots a blip. Then it uses the time to predict where that blip should be a moment later, and it looks only inside a small window around that spot. {p} If the target shows up in the window, it's real: lock on. {p} If the window is empty, it's a false alarm: ignore it.

shots.src: US GAO, IMTEC-92-26 (1992): Patriot Missile Defense, Software Problem Led to System Failure at Dhahran · Appendix II
shots.narration: Ninety-five billionths of a second sounds like nothing. {p} But the battery had been running nonstop for over a hundred hours. That's three point six million ticks. {p} After a hundred hours, the clock was off by a third of a second. {p} A Scud travels about one point seven kilometers every second. {pp} The radar's tracking window had slid six hundred and eighty-seven meters away from where the missile actually was. {p} It looked, saw nothing, and decided there was no missile.

shots.src: US GAO, IMTEC-92-26 (1992): Patriot Missile Defense, Software Problem Led to System Failure at Dhahran
shots.title: Dhahran, February 1991
shots.narration: The worst part? {p} They knew. On February eleventh, Israeli data showed the tracking window drifting after just eight hours of nonstop running. {p} A corrected version of the software was released. {p} Then, on February twenty-first, the Army warned that very long run times could shift the window. {p} But it didn't say how long was too long. {pp} The fix reached Dhahran on February twenty-sixth. {p} One day too late.

items.text: Feb 11 · Israeli data: drift after 8 hours
Feb 21 · warning: “very long run times”… how long?

shots.title: YouTube views, Gangnam Style (2014)
shots.unit: the biggest number a 32-bit counter can hold

wrap.text: one more view in a 32-bit counter

notes.text: YouTube moved to 64 bits in time

shots.narration: The second kind of error isn't about tiny numbers. It's about big ones. {p} In 2014, Gangnam Style was about to pass two point one billion views, and YouTube noticed a problem. {p} Its view counter used a thirty-two-bit number, and the biggest number that fits is two billion, one hundred forty-seven million, four hundred eighty-three thousand, six hundred forty-seven. {p} One more view, and the counter wraps around to minus two billion. {p} YouTube switched to sixty-four bits just in time.

shots.title: Ariane 5 · flight 501 · 4 June 1996
shots.narration: Ariane 5 wasn't so lucky. {p} June fourth, 1996. Europe's new heavy rocket lifts off on its very first flight, carrying four science satellites. {p} Thirty-seven seconds later, it swings sideways, and blows itself up.

shots.label: 64-bit number → 16-bit box
shots.narration: The cause? A piece of navigation code reused from the older Ariane 4. {p} It took a sixty-four-bit number, the rocket's horizontal bias, and squeezed it into a sixteen-bit box. {p} Ariane 5 flew faster than Ariane 4, the number was too big, {p} and the navigation computer crashed. Then the backup crashed too, for exactly the same reason.

shots.title: Ariane 501, second by second
shots.narration: What happened next took about two seconds. {p} With both navigation computers down, the flight computer read their error message as if it were real flight data. {p} It swung the engine nozzles all the way to one side. {p} The rocket turned sideways at high speed, the air started tearing it apart, and it triggered its own self-destruct.

items.text: T+36.7 s · both navigation computers crash
T+37 s · error message read as flight data
T+37 s · nozzles swing to full deflection
T+39 s · rocket breaks up, self-destructs

shots.src: Ariane 501 Inquiry Board report · estimated loss
shots.title: The cruel detail
shots.narration: And here's the cruel detail. {p} That piece of code was only needed before liftoff. {p} On Ariane 5, after launch, it served no purpose at all. {pp} More than three hundred and seventy million dollars, lost to a number that didn't fit in a box nobody needed.

shots.title: Vancouver Stock Exchange index, 1982
shots.narration: Now the strangest one. {p} In January 1982, the Vancouver Stock Exchange launched a new index, starting at one thousand. {p} It was recalculated about three thousand times a day. {p} And every single time, the computer didn't round the result. {p} It just cut it off after three decimals.

shots.title: Lost to cutting, Jan 1982 → Nov 1983
shots.narration: Each cut was tiny, less than a thousandth of a point. {p} But three thousand cuts a day add up. {p} The index was quietly losing more than a point every trading day, while the actual stocks were doing fine. {pp} And nobody noticed, because a market going down slowly doesn't look like a bug. {p} It looks like a bad economy.

shots.title: Same market, November 1983
shots.narration: After twenty-two months, by November 1983, the index read five hundred twenty-four point eight. {p} On paper, the market had lost almost half its value. {pp} When they finally recalculated it properly, the real number was one thousand ninety-eight point nine. {p} It had actually gone up.

shots.title: Unix clock, seconds since January 1, 1970
shots.unit: last second that fits: 03:14:07 UTC, January 19, 2038
shots.narration: And one of these errors is still ticking. {p} Billions of computers count time as seconds since January first, 1970. {p} In a thirty-two-bit number, that count runs out at three fourteen and seven seconds a.m., on January nineteenth, 2038. {p} One second later, the clock wraps around to December 1901.

Most modern systems already count in sixty-four bits, which lasts about two hundred and ninety-two billion years. {p} But old machines, embedded chips and forgotten code are everywhere, in cars, factories, routers and power systems, and many of them will still be running in 2038. {p} So the lesson isn't that computers are bad at math. {p} It's that every number lives in a box, {pp} and somebody has to check that the box is big enough.

items.text: Every number lives in a box.

shots.narration: Next time: another number that isn't what it looks like. Why a one-terabyte drive only shows nine hundred thirty-one gigabytes. {p} Subscribe so you don't miss it. I'm How It Ticks. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Tiny Math Errors That Cost Lives and Millions
yt.description:
Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 on a computer? The same kind of tiny error made a Patriot missile miss in 1991, blew up Ariane 5 in 1996, and made the Vancouver Stock Exchange "lose" half its value. And one of these bugs is still ticking: 2038.

Sources: US GAO report IMTEC-92-26 (1992); Ariane 501 Inquiry Board report (1996); Vancouver Stock Exchange index history; CBC/BBC (Dec 2014) on YouTube's 64-bit counter; IEEE 754 floating point.
